segments.original: The devil made an early debut in cinema. In Le Manoir du diable (1896), director Georges Méliès (1861-1938) plays Mephistopheles. The best version of the Faust legend is still Faust (1926), by F. W. Murnau (1888-1931), but pacts with the devil have appeared in other films such as The Devil and Daniel Webster (1941) and The Devil's Advocate (1997). Many dramas, such as Wall Street (1987) and The Devil Wears Prada (2006), boil down to a new guise for the Faust story, adorned with the specific concerns of their era. Devil worship crept into cinema mainly as a threat, as in The Seventh Victim (1943), whose New York coven prefigures Ira Levin's, as well as in Hammer's boisterous The Devil Rides Out (1967). One of cinema's best devils was Robert De Niro (b. 1943) in Angel Heart (1987).

segments.original: Beyond the supernatural evil of The Haunting (1963) and the alien invaders of The Day of the Triffids (1962), horror cinema also took on a human face. With The Birds (1963), Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980) once again subverted what audiences expect of a heroine.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The classic female lead in horror films is the virginal blonde dressed in white who acts as a moral compass: the kindhearted Mina survives Dracula, whereas having sex can have sinister consequences, as happened to Mia Farrow in Rosemary's Baby. Unlike the vast majority of female leads in horror films, Tippi Hedren's (b. 1930) Melanie in The Birds is no wilting violet, but a confident woman who pursues a man all the way to his front door. With that, female characters came to have a far greater range than their mere terrified stares.

With a core trio formed by director Terence Fisher (1904-1980) and actors Christopher Lee and Peter Cushing, Hammer became Britain's leading studio, regularly producing films such as Dracula: Prince of Darkness (1966) and Frankenstein Must Be Destroyed (1969) and, at its peak, The Devil Rides Out (1968), with a screenplay by Richard Matheson (1926-2013).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In Western cinemas, the 1960s were the era when horror films were respected as art. However, it was also the decade in which the genre began to lose focus. The studios realized they could churn out endless sequels and crude imitations. The horror film became a cheap commodity and the drive-in became a home for exploitation fare. Nevertheless, this type of film gave 1960s filmmaking a reach and scope that flourished until the arrival and saturation of the B-movie market of the Jason genre.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: George Romero's work deserves full credit on its own: the film is a landmark of low-budget cinema that not only establishes the threat of the undead horde but also delivers tension and action combined with a solid layer of social commentary, featuring a Black hero who defies the stereotypes of the time - and a treacherous ending with timeless impact. The feature also doesn't hold back on violence, something that caught 1960s audiences off guard, especially considering there was no age-rating system to control who watched it in theaters: "The movie had stopped being delightfully scary about halfway through, and had become unexpectedly terrifying," wrote Roger Ebert, critic for the Chicago Sun-Times. "There was a little girl across the aisle from me, maybe nine years old, who was sitting very still in her seat and crying."

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: But what elevated Night of the Living Dead from a great film into a true cultural phenomenon has to do not only with its content but also with its distribution. As it happens, the film was originally called Night of the Flesh Eaters (or A Noite dos Devoradores de Carne, in a loose Portuguese translation) but, since the name was very similar to that of The Flesh Eaters (1964), the distributor Walter Reade Organization asked for the title to be changed to Night of the Living Dead. The sudden change came with a slip: to secure copyright on an audiovisual work at the time, the copyright symbol (©) had to appear in the film's opening. When the title was changed, the production forgot to include the notice of intellectual property. Just a tiny mistake, right?

The sudden change came with a slip: to secure copyright on an audiovisual work at the time, the copyright symbol (©) had to appear in the film's opening. When the title was changed, the production forgot to include the notice of intellectual property. Just a tiny mistake, right?

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In fact, the absence of the symbol meant that Night of the Living Dead was released straight into the public domain; in other words, anyone could simply get a copy and screen it publicly as many times as they wanted, even charging admission. While this may have hurt the original distributor's pocket, since it wasn't collecting the box-office takings, the accident allowed the film to be widely shown at smaller events, small theaters, drive-ins and every kind of venue that wanted to screen the much-talked-about indie horror.

segments.original: Moreover, the public domain also allows different creators to contribute to the characters and concepts of the work in question. Basically any filmmaker could now use Romero's zombies in their projects - and that is exactly what happened, with a veritable infestation of films about the walking dead. The best example of this perhaps comes from Italy, a prolific low-budget film industry, which launched major filmmakers through imitations and reinterpretations of the American film, such as Zombi 2 (Zombie Flesh Eaters, 1979), an unofficial sequel to Night of the Living Dead by horror master Lucio Fulci (1927-1996).
